newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin slates extra revenue for deficit cuts - paper.
newsitem.headline: Jospin slates extra revenue for deficit cuts - paper.

text.p: French budget instruction letters sent to ministers by Prime Minister Lionel Jospin say any extra state revenue generated by higher-than-expected economic growth should be earmarked above all to reducing public deficits, the daily Liberation said, quoting one of the budget letters.

"Any additional revenues that could flow from higher growth should, as a priority, be deployed to reduce the budget deficit, which calls for a tough stance on public spending management," Liberation quoted the letter as saying.

The paper said the government had left itself some room for manoeuvre by not saying any additional receipts would have to be used "exclusively" to cut the deficit if growth was far stronger than expected.
Liberation said the letter asks ministers to hold 1998 civil service staff levels at the same level as in 1997 and to avoid proposing any specific measures related to their personnel.
"The number of civil servants will be maintained in 1998 at its 1997 level..."Moreover, I am asking you not to propose, for 1998, any specific measures related to your personnel," it said.

The letter said ministries should come up with suggestions on how the new government could change spending commitments undertaken by the previous centre-right government to help reduce the state's deficit.

"Finding room for manoeuvre, to finance the new government's priorities and carry on with deficit reduction, may thus lead us to question some of these commitments. I am waiting for your proposals," the budget letter said, according to the paper.

The letter called on ministries to find more efficient ways of spending given the government's commitment to implement new measures without boosting the overall level of state spending, the paper said.

"As you know, the government has committed itself to implementing new priorities without raising overall public spending. The state therefore needs to spend better, to avoid increasing payroll charges and to stick to the deficit-cutting path."
